title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 67 (Restrictions on financial assistance for purchase of own shares)

content.overview: Section 67 restricts a public company from giving financial assistance, directly or indirectly, for purchase of or subscription to its own shares or those of its holding company, subject to stated exceptions.
content.glance: Section 67 restricts a public company from giving financial assistance, directly or indirectly, for purchase of or subscription to its own shares or those of its holding company, subject to stated exceptions.
content.study: The prohibition targets loans, guarantees and other financial assistance that would let a company fund acquisition of its own shares. Private companies are outside the principal prohibition, subject to later exemptions that must be checked in the notification in force. Exceptions recognised in the section include lending by a banking company in the ordinary course, provision of money for an employee share scheme, and loans to employees other than directors or key managerial personnel within the stated salary limit to buy fully paid shares. A transaction structured through a subsidiary or a friendly party can still be indirect assistance. Breach attracts the penalty in the section and may also engage fraud provisions if dishonest intent is proved.

examples.title: Employee scheme
examples.body: Money provided under a qualifying employee scheme for fully paid shares can fall within the exception.

examples.title: Routed loan
examples.body: A loan to a relative of a promoter to buy the company's shares can be indirect assistance.

distinctions: Section 67 restricts assistance for purchase. Section 68 is the company's own buy-back. Section 185 restricts loans to directors and is a separate gate.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Does s. 67 apply in the same way to every private company?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: The principal prohibition is addressed to public companies. Private-company exemptions must be confirmed from the notification in force; do not assume a blanket exemption.
